design_detail: Randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled, three-period within-participant crossover trial (NCT04201197) at the Johns Hopkins Behavioral Pharmacology Research Unit, January 2021 to March 2022. 18 healthy adults with past cannabis experience and no use for at least 30 days completed three 14-hour outpatient sessions at least one week apart, in an order set by a randomized Latin square, eating a brownie with placebo, a THC-dominant whole-plant extract (20 mg THC, no CBD) or a CBD-dominant whole-plant extract (20 mg THC with 640 mg CBD) (study conditions). In every session a cocktail of five cytochrome P450 probe drugs (caffeine, omeprazole, losartan, dextromethorphan, midazolam) was swallowed 30 minutes after the brownie, because the trial's primary aim was cannabinoid–drug interactions; this paper reports the secondary outcomes: THC pharmacokinetics and subjective, cognitive and cardiovascular effects over 24 hours.
can_establish: That in these conditions (oral extracts in a brownie, the probe cocktail given in every session, healthy adults who rarely use cannabis), the CBD-dominant extract produced higher plasma THC and much higher 11-OH-THC exposure, and stronger subjective, cognitive and heart-rate effects, than the THC-dominant extract carrying the same nominal THC dose.
cannot_establish: The effect of CBD alone (no CBD-only condition) or of lower CBD doses, inhaled cannabis, regular cannabis use or CBD taken separately from THC; whether the stronger effects came only from altered THC metabolism rather than from the probe drugs (whose levels are not reported here) or from the extract's other cannabinoids; or that CBD increases anxiety or sleepiness compared with THC alone (these differences were not significant).

sample.recruitment: Advertisement: media advertisements and word of mouth (Methods › Participants).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Age 18 to 50; body mass index 18 to 34; past experience with cannabis; no cannabis use in the 30 days before the first session; negative urine drug tests at screening and at the start of every session; not pregnant or nursing; no allergy to cannabinoids or study drugs; good health on blood tests, history and examination (Methods › Participants).
sample.demographics: 11 men and 7 women; mean age 30 (SD 7) years, weight 78 (SD 12) kg, BMI 25 (SD 2); 12 White, 3 Black and 3 Asian, all non-Hispanic; mean 124 (SD 80) days since last self-reported cannabis use, median 93, range 39 to 295 (Results, 1st paragraph).
sample.attrition: 36 consented, 22 were randomized and 18 completed; participants who dropped out were replaced and only completers were analysed (Methods › Study Design and Procedures, 1st paragraph; Results, 1st paragraph). Reasons for dropping out and the conditions they had received are given only in the flow diagram (Figure 1), an image that was not viewable in this reading.
sample.selection_effects: Healthy volunteers with past but infrequent cannabis use, recruited by advertisement and willing to take a probe-drug cocktail in three long sessions; people with regular use, older adults, people with health problems and people on other medicines were not represented.

exposure.measurement: Supervised ingestion of a brownie prepared and dispensed by a pharmacist (participants and staff blinded); plasma THC, 11-OH-THC and THC-COOH by liquid chromatography–tandem mass spectrometry at baseline and 0.25 to 24 hours after the cocktail (Methods › Study Design and Procedures, 1st paragraph; Outcome Measures, 1st and 2nd paragraphs).
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Study conditions only: one brownie per session, oral, after a standard low-fat breakfast: placebo (ethanol vehicle), THC-dominant extract (20 mg THC, no CBD) or CBD-dominant extract (20 mg THC with 640 mg CBD); probe cocktail of caffeine 100 mg, omeprazole 20 mg, losartan 25 mg, dextromethorphan 30 mg and midazolam 2 mg 30 minutes later in every session; at least one week between sessions (Methods › Study Design and Procedures, 1st and 2nd paragraphs). Extracts from the NIDA Drug Supply Program, decarboxylated, made under cGMP: the THC-dominant extract held 70% THC, 2.7% CBG, 1.5% CBN, under 1% THCV, CBC and Δ8-THC and no detectable CBD; the CBD-dominant extract held 59.3% CBD, 2.1% CBC, 2.0% THC, 1.1% CBG and under 1% CBN, THCV and Δ8-THC (Methods › Cannabis Extracts and Study Drugs).
exposure.polysubstance: Urine drug tests negative at screening and before each session; participants were told to avoid cannabis and cannabinoid products, tobacco, caffeine, grapefruit and other fruit juices and not to change medicines or supplements throughout the study (Methods › Study Design and Procedures, 1st paragraph). Alcohol testing is not mentioned. Within sessions, the probe drugs (including the sedative midazolam, dextromethorphan and caffeine) were taken with every brownie.
exposure.abstinence_at_testing: At least 30 days without cannabis before the first session by self-report (mean 124 days), with negative urine drug tests before every session; no THC metabolites were detectable after the placebo brownie (Methods › Participants; Results, 1st paragraph; Methods › Statistical Analysis, 1st paragraph).

comparison.controls: Within-person: each participant had placebo, THC-dominant and CBD-dominant sessions, all with the probe cocktail. The key comparison for CBD is CBD-dominant against THC-dominant extract at the same nominal THC dose.
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Not applicable for the within-person comparisons; anxiety-proneness and other traits that might change responses were not measured or analysed.
comparison.controls_other_drug_use: Same participants in all conditions; the probe cocktail was identical across sessions.

outcomes.instruments: Plasma THC, 11-OH-THC and THC-COOH: Cmax, AUC (trapezoidal) and AUC ratios. Drug Effect Questionnaire (0–100 visual analogue items: drug effect, pleasant, unpleasant, liking, sick, heart racing, anxious or nervous, relaxed, paranoid, sleepy, alert, irritable, restless, hungry, craving, dry mouth, dry or red eyes, memory, routine tasks and others). Digit symbol substitution task, modified paced serial addition task, divided attention task; heart rate and blood pressure. Ratings and vital signs at baseline and 0.25 to 24 hours, tasks at baseline and 0.5 to 24 hours after the cocktail (Methods › Outcome Measures, 1st to 4th paragraphs).
outcomes.validity_norms: The questionnaire and tasks are described as sensitive to acute THC and cannabis effects in the group's earlier studies; participants were trained on the tasks at screening to reduce practice effects (Methods › Outcome Measures, 3rd and 4th paragraphs).
outcomes.operationalization: Effects are expressed as peak change from each session's baseline; comparisons between conditions are Tukey tests on peak change after two-way repeated-measures ANOVA (dose × time); pharmacokinetic comparisons are paired t tests between the two active conditions (Methods › Statistical Analysis, 1st and 2nd paragraphs).
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: Tukey adjustment across the three condition contrasts within each outcome; no adjustment across the 27 effect outcomes in the Table (21 questionnaire items, 3 tasks, 3 vital signs) and the 9 pharmacokinetic measures (Methods › Statistical Analysis, 2nd paragraph).
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Double-blind: a pharmacist prepared and dispensed all study drugs; plasma analysed in a separate laboratory. THC's effects would make active sessions recognisable against placebo; the two active brownies held the same nominal THC dose.

analysis.effect_sizes: Pharmacokinetics, CBD-dominant against THC-dominant extract, mean (SD), units not printed in the text (Results, 2nd paragraph): THC Cmax 14.8 (5.5) against 8.2 (4.0), d = 1.4 (95% CI 0.4 to 2.4); 11-OH-THC Cmax 53.9 (22.6) against 4.5 (1.9), d = 3.1 (1.7 to 4.4); THC-COOH Cmax 118.6 (44.8) against 45.1 (18.5), d = 2.1 (0.9 to 3.3); THC AUC 84.9 (29.38) against 33.3 (16.9), d = 2.2 (1.0 to 3.4); 11-OH-THC AUC 349.0 (137.1) against 34.0 (16.4), d = 3.2 (1.8 to 4.6); THC-COOH AUC 1030.0 (456.4) against 445.7 (196.2), d = 2.8 (1.5 to 4.1); all P < .001. Editors' arithmetic from these means: THC Cmax about 1.8 times and AUC about 2.5 times higher, 11-OH-THC Cmax about 12 times and AUC about 10 times higher with the CBD-dominant extract. Effects, mean peak change from baseline (SD), placebo / THC-dominant / CBD-dominant (Table): drug effect 9.4 (27.8) / 59.2 (31.1) / 72.8 (25.9); unpleasant 4.1 (12.9) / 19.6 (23.4) / 38.6 (28.0); sick 3.4 (9.0) / 11.6 (18.9) / 26.1 (22.3); anxious or nervous 4.1 (14.8) / 13.3 (20.2) / 23.9 (29.1); paranoid -0.1 (8.0) / 12.0 (16.8) / 23.4 (28.8); sleepy or tired -12.9 (38.3) / 21.0 (42.9) / 42.6 (42.3); memory impairment 5.6 (10.0) / 27.4 (31.7) / 37.8 (32.6); difficulty with routine tasks 6.6 (13.4) / 30.3 (27.8) / 46.7 (30.3); paced serial addition -1.1 (14.2) / -6.6 (19.1) / -22.7 (24.6); divided attention -2.1 (9.4) / 15.9 (24.7) / 32.7 (39.2) (higher is worse); heart rate -4.4 (12.4) / 10.1 (14.1) / 25.4 (20.9) beats per minute. Many printed Cohen d values for effect outcomes do not match these means and SDs (see reporting issues), so the means, SDs and Tukey P values are the safer figures. Mean times of peak effect were later with the CBD-dominant extract for most ratings (for drug effect 2.9 h against 2.1 h, Table), not tested statistically.
analysis.covariates: None (within-person comparisons of change from each session's baseline).
analysis.preregistration_detail: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT04201197; the trial protocol is Supplement 2 (a PDF, not opened). The trial's primary outcome was losartan AUC (cannabinoid–drug interaction), to be reported elsewhere; the outcomes in this paper are secondary. The registry record was not read, so registered and reported secondary outcomes were not compared.
analysis.selective_reporting: Probe-drug results, including midazolam and dextromethorphan exposure under each extract, are deferred to later papers although they bear on the effects reported here. The text and the Table disagree on several effect results (see reporting issues). All PD items are tabulated for all three conditions, which limits selective reporting within this paper.
analysis.power: Sample size set for the primary outcome (18 participants, 84% power for a 25% change in losartan AUC); for the effect outcomes the authors cite expected effect sizes of about 0.87 to 1.0 from their laboratory's earlier studies. Not powered for sex differences (Methods › Statistical Analysis, 1st paragraph; Limitations).

interpretation_gap.results_show: With the probe cocktail in every session, the CBD-dominant extract (20 mg THC with 640 mg CBD) gave higher plasma THC and far higher 11-OH-THC than the THC-dominant extract, and, against THC-dominant extract, higher ratings of drug effect, unpleasant, sick, red eyes, memory trouble and difficulty with routine tasks, worse paced serial addition and divided attention, and a larger rise in heart rate. Anxious or nervous, paranoid, sleepy, pleasant and liking ratings and the digit symbol task did not differ significantly between the two active extracts.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract says the CBD-dominant extract increased self-reported anxiety, sedation and memory difficulty compared with both THC-dominant extract and placebo (Abstract › Results); by the Table, anxiety and sleepiness differed from placebo only. The Key Points say the effects appear mediated by CBD inhibiting the metabolism of THC and 11-OH-THC, and the abstract's Conclusions and Relevance call this the likely mechanism; no mediation was tested, the CBD extract also carried other cannabinoids, and the probe drugs (including midazolam) were given in every session with their levels unreported, which the Limitations concede may have contributed to the effects. The abstract presents the result as contradicting common claims that CBD attenuates THC's adverse effects, from one high oral CBD dose in one product ratio.

timeline.event: Haney et al. (2016): oral CBD did not alter the subjective, reinforcing or cardiovascular effects of smoked cannabis (title from the project's BeforeDuring list; not read for this card).
Systematic review of how CBD influences the acute effects of THC in humans (on the project's BeforeDuring list, Tier A; not read for this card).
This trial: oral CBD-dominant extract raised THC and 11-OH-THC exposure and strengthened several effects compared with a THC-dominant extract at the same THC dose.
Chester et al. (2026): systematic review and meta-analysis of whether co-administered CBD changes plasma THC and its active metabolite (on the project's BeforeDuring list; not read for this card).

replication.where_it_stands: The paper describes earlier laboratory findings on CBD with THC as equivocal (attenuation, potentiation or no change), mostly with inhaled or intravenous dosing (Introduction, 2nd and 3rd paragraphs). It is the study in the project's map showing oral CBD raising THC levels and effects; a later meta-analysis of plasma THC with CBD (Chester et al., 2026) and further crossover trials are listed but not appraised here.

Three authors report fees or contract work from cannabis and cannabinoid companies, outside this work. Recorded as a flag for closer reading, not as a reason to discount the results.

what_would_settle_it: A randomized crossover trial without co-administered probe drugs that fixes the THC dose and varies the CBD dose (including amounts found in consumer products and a CBD-only condition), uses single-cannabinoid preparations to separate CBD from other cannabinoids, includes both infrequent and regular cannabis use, measures THC and 11-OH-THC, and pre-registers anxiety and paranoia as outcomes.

domains.domain: Bias arising from the randomization process
domains.note: Condition order assigned by a randomized Latin square; a pharmacist prepared and dispensed all study drugs, keeping staff and participants blind. Each session had its own baseline.

domains.domain: Bias arising from period and carryover effects (crossover)
domains.note: At least one week between sessions; no THC or metabolites were detectable after the placebo brownie, which argues against THC carry-over. Period effects and the balance of sequences among completers after replacement of dropouts are not reported.

domains.domain: Bias due to deviations from intended interventions
domains.note: Supervised dosing in the laboratory, double-blind. Active sessions are recognisable against placebo, but the two active brownies carried the same nominal THC dose. The probe cocktail was part of the protocol in every session, so it is a matter of applicability (and of mechanism) rather than a deviation.

domains.domain: Bias due to missing outcome data
domains.note: 4 of 22 randomized participants (18%) did not complete and were replaced; only completers were analysed, and the reasons and the conditions received before dropping out are only in an image that could not be viewed. If dropping out followed strong effects in one condition, differences between conditions could be under- or overstated.

domains.domain: Bias in measurement of the outcome
domains.note: Plasma assays and computerized tasks are objective; self-ratings were made under double-blind conditions (a pharmacist prepared and dispensed all study drugs); no check of blinding is reported, which matters little here because the two active brownies carried the same nominal THC dose.

domains.domain: Bias in selection of the reported result
domains.note: Registered trial whose primary outcome is reported elsewhere; the registry was not read here. Many outcomes without correction across outcomes; the abstract's summary of anxiety and sedation does not match the Table; many printed effect sizes do not match the printed data.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: Randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled crossover with supervised dosing and objective pharmacokinetics: the large rise in THC and 11-OH-THC exposure with the CBD-dominant extract is credible for these conditions. Concerns are the completers-only analysis after replacing 4 of 22 randomized participants, the unreported probe-drug levels in a design that gave midazolam and dextromethorphan in every session, and inconsistent reporting of effect results. The card may be cited for: in 18 healthy adults with infrequent cannabis use, 20 mg oral THC taken in a CBD-dominant extract (640 mg CBD) produced higher THC and 11-OH-THC levels and stronger drug-effect, unpleasant, sick, memory, task, cognitive and heart-rate effects than the same nominal THC dose in a THC-dominant extract, with a probe-drug cocktail given in every session. It should not be cited for CBD increasing anxiety, paranoia or sleepiness compared with THC alone (not significant), for lower CBD doses, inhaled cannabis, regular use, or CBD on its own.

key_findings.finding: Design and sample: randomized, double-blind, within-participant crossover; 18 of 22 randomized healthy adults (11 men, 7 women, mean age 30) with past cannabis experience and no use for at least 30 days completed three sessions at least one week apart, with brownies of placebo, THC-dominant extract (20 mg THC) or CBD-dominant extract (20 mg THC + 640 mg CBD) (study conditions), each followed 30 minutes later by a five-drug CYP probe cocktail.
key_findings.locator: Abstract › Design, Setting, and Participants; Interventions; Methods › Study Design and Procedures, 1st paragraph; Results, 1st paragraph

key_findings.finding: Plasma exposure with the CBD-dominant against the THC-dominant extract: THC Cmax 14.8 (SD 5.5) against 8.2 (4.0), THC AUC 84.9 (29.38) against 33.3 (16.9); 11-OH-THC Cmax 53.9 (22.6) against 4.5 (1.9), AUC 349.0 (137.1) against 34.0 (16.4); THC-COOH Cmax 118.6 (44.8) against 45.1 (18.5), AUC 1030.0 (456.4) against 445.7 (196.2); all P < .001, n = 18. Higher 11-OH-THC:THC and lower THC-COOH:11-OH-THC AUC ratios (4.5 against 1.2; 3.1 against 14.4).
key_findings.note: Units are not printed in the text (eTable 1 in Supplement 1, a PDF, was not opened). Editors' arithmetic: THC Cmax about 1.8-fold, 11-OH-THC Cmax about 12-fold higher.

key_findings.finding: The placebo brownie with the probe cocktail produced no significant change in any effect measure over time.

Against the THC-dominant extract, the CBD-dominant extract produced larger peak changes from baseline in ratings of drug effect (72.8 against 59.2), unpleasant (38.6 against 19.6), sick (26.1 against 11.6), dry or red eyes (28.8 against 15.9; 28.7 in the text), memory impairment (37.8 against 27.4) and difficulty performing routine tasks (46.7 against 30.3) (Tukey P < .05).
key_findings.locator: Results, 3rd paragraph; Table, rows marked c

key_findings.finding: No significant difference between the two active extracts in pleasant (57.9 against 55.9) or liking ratings, anxious or nervous (23.9 against 13.3), paranoid (23.4 against 12.0), sleepy or tired (42.6 against 21.0), heart racing or restless ratings; anxious or nervous, sleepy and paranoid were higher than placebo after the CBD-dominant extract.
key_findings.locator: Table (rows without the c marker); Results, 3rd paragraph
key_findings.note: The abstract states that anxiety and sedation were increased compared with both THC-dominant extract and placebo; the Table supports only the comparison with placebo.

key_findings.finding: Cognitive and cardiovascular effects: against the THC-dominant extract, the CBD-dominant extract gave fewer correct paced serial additions (-22.7 against -6.6, P = .049) and greater divided-attention tracking error (32.7 against 15.9, P = .04), and a larger rise in heart rate (25.4 against 10.1 beats per minute, P = .001); the digit symbol task did not differ significantly between the active extracts; blood pressure showed no effects.
key_findings.locator: Results, 4th paragraph; Table, Cognitive measures and Physiological measures rows

key_findings.finding: The CBD-dominant extract also contained 2.1% CBC and 1.1% CBG (THC-dominant extract: 2.7% CBG, 1.5% CBN, no detectable CBD), so the comparison is between two whole-plant extracts rather than THC with and without pure CBD.
key_findings.locator: Methods › Cannabis Extracts and Study Drugs, 1st paragraph
key_findings.note: Editors' arithmetic: about 1.0 to 1.1 g of the CBD-dominant extract supplies the stated doses, bringing roughly 21 to 23 mg CBC and 11 to 12 mg CBG, against under 1 mg of each minor cannabinoid from the roughly 29 mg of THC-dominant extract.

key_findings.finding: The authors' limitations: a single dose of THC and of CBD, no CBD-only condition; outcomes measured with the CYP probe cocktail, which may have contributed to the behavioural effects in the active conditions; not powered to detect sex differences.

reporting_issues.issue: The abstract says the CBD-dominant extract increased self-reported anxiety and sedation compared with both the THC-dominant extract and placebo, but the Table marks anxious or nervous (23.9 against 13.3) and sleepy or tired (42.6 against 21.0) as different from placebo only, not from the THC-dominant extract; the Results text names only unpleasant, sick and red-eye ratings among adverse items as higher than with THC alone.
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML (Abstract › Results; Table; Results, 3rd paragraph)
reporting_issues.consequence: The trial does not show that CBD made the experience more anxious or sleepy than the same THC dose alone; the abstract should not be cited for that.

reporting_issues.issue: Days since last cannabis use are given as mean 86 (SD 66) in the abstract and mean 124 (SD 80), median 93, range 39 to 295, in the Results.
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor; the Results figure is the detailed one.

reporting_issues.issue: The text says that the THC-dominant extract increased only dry mouth among the adverse ratings compared with placebo, while the Table marks unpleasant, paranoid, sleepy or tired, irritable, heart racing and throat irritation as significantly higher than placebo after the THC-dominant extract.
reporting_issues.consequence: The adverse effects of THC alone are understated in the text; use the Table.

reporting_issues.issue: Printed Cohen d values: for plasma Cmax and AUC (except THC-COOH AUC) and for drug effect they match a pooled-SD calculation from the printed means and SDs, but many others do not (editors' calculation): pleasant printed 1.7 and 2.4 (about 1.5 and 1.6), paranoid 2.4 (about 1.1), sleepy 0.7 (about 1.4), dry mouth 0.9 (about 1.7), heart rate against placebo 0.7 (about 1.7), THC-COOH AUC 2.8 (about 1.7). Pleasant and paranoid repeat the d and interval printed for drug effect; the unpleasant interval (0.4 to 2.1) is lopsided around 1.7; and several intervals include zero next to P < .001 (drug effect against THC alone, d 0.5, -0.5 to 1.4; THC-COOH:THC ratio, d -0.31, -1.2 to 0.6). Memory and routine tasks against the THC-dominant extract also match (0.3 and 0.6), but two further contrasts against it do not: dry or red eyes, printed 1.0 (about 0.4), and paced serial addition, printed −0.5 (about −0.7); and intervals that include zero sit beside P < .05 against the THC-dominant extract for memory (0.3, −0.6 to 1.2, P = .03), routine tasks (0.6, −0.4 to 1.5, P = .02), paced serial addition (−0.5, −1.3 to 0.2, P = .049), divided attention (0.4, −0.4 to 1.5, P = .04) and heart rate (0.7, −0.1 to 1.8, P = .001) (editors' calculation).
reporting_issues.consequence: The printed effect sizes and their intervals cannot be relied on for the effect outcomes; cite means, SDs and the Tukey or paired-test P values instead. The intervals appear not to reflect the within-person design.

reporting_issues.issue: Value slips between text and Table: the paced serial addition result against placebo is printed with SD 34.6 (Table and later text 24.6) and its comparator is labelled THC-dominant with the placebo value (-1.1, SD 14.2); dry mouth after THC-dominant extract is 35.9 in the text and 35.0 in the Table; dry or red eyes after CBD-dominant extract is 28.7 in the text and 28.8 in the Table; the drug-effect comparison of CBD-dominant extract with placebo carries two P values (P < .001; P = .003).
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor; the Table values are internally consistent and are preferred.

reporting_issues.issue: By the stated composition of the CBD-dominant extract (59.3% CBD, 2.0% THC), 640 mg CBD comes with about 21.6 mg THC, and 20 mg THC with about 593 mg CBD (editors' calculation); measured brownie contents are not reported, although periodic testing is described.
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML (Methods › Cannabis Extracts and Study Drugs)
reporting_issues.consequence: The THC dose in the CBD-dominant condition may have been up to about 8% higher than 20 mg; too small to explain an 1.8-fold THC Cmax difference, but the two conditions were not certainly matched for THC.

reporting_issues.issue: The levels of the probe drugs (including the sedative midazolam and dextromethorphan) under each extract are not reported in this paper, although CBD's inhibition of the same enzymes is the proposed mechanism and the authors note the cocktail may have contributed to the effects.
reporting_issues.consequence: Part of the extra sedation and impairment with the CBD-dominant extract could reflect higher probe-drug exposure; the attribution to THC and 11-OH-THC alone is not established by this paper.

reporting_issues.issue: Peak times in the Table range from 0 to at most 6.0 hours for every measure in every condition, although ratings, tasks and vital signs were recorded up to 24 hours after the cocktail; the time course, and so how long the stronger effects lasted, is shown only in Figures 3 and 4, which were not viewable in either reading, and no test of peak time is reported.
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML (Table; Methods › Outcome Measures, 1st paragraph; Figures 3 and 4)
reporting_issues.consequence: The card cannot state how long the effects lasted; the later mean peak with the CBD-dominant extract (2.9 against 2.1 hours for drug effect) is descriptive only.
